questions.question: What is the Taylor series of a real analytic function $f$ around $x = a$?
What changes in the Taylor series of $f$ when the centre moves from $0$ to $a$?
In the Taylor series around $a$, what is the coefficient of $(x-a)^2$?
Which is the Maclaurin series of $\mathrm{e}^x$?
What does real analyticity at $x = a$ guarantee in the proposition?
options: That $f$ agrees with its Taylor series on the whole domain $E$.
That $f$ agrees with its Taylor series on some interval $(a-r,a+r)$.
That the Taylor series converges near $a$, possibly to another function.
That $f$ is a polynomial on some interval $(a-r,a+r)$.

questions.question: When does a formal Taylor series necessarily converge to the original function?
options: Every smooth function equals its Taylor series near every point of its domain.
A smooth function equals its Taylor series wherever that series converges near $a$.
It equals $f$ whenever the coefficients $f^{(n)}(a)/n!$ tend to $0$.
A smooth function has a formal Taylor series; it equals $f$ only if $f$ is analytic.

questions.question: For a Taylor series around $a = 2$, which factor appears in the $n$-th term?
In the generalized binomial expansion, what is the coefficient of $x^2$ in $(1+x)^r$?
A function has a Taylor series at $a$. Which extra property is needed before the series can safely be used as the function near $a$?
options: The Taylor series must terminate after finitely many nonzero terms.
$f$ must be infinitely differentiable at $a$, and nothing more.
The Taylor series must converge to $f$ on the neighbourhood.
The centre must be $a=0$, making it a Maclaurin series.

questions.question: Why is the condition that $a$ is an interior point relevant to the statement?
options: It forces $E$ to be an open interval of the form $(a-r,a+r)$.
It guarantees the Taylor series converges at every $x\in E$.
It ensures $f$ is real analytic at $a$ without further conditions.
It gives an interval $(a-r,a+r)\subseteq E$ for the expansion.

questions.question: A function is real analytic at $a = 0$ and has derivatives $f^{(n)}(0) = 1$ for all $n \geq 0$. Which Taylor series is obtained?
Which proposed conclusion is justified if $f$ is real analytic at $a$?
options: The Taylor series equals $f$ only at $x = a$, not on any interval around $a$.
There is some $r \gt 0$ such that $f(x) = \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty}f^{(n)}(a)(x-a)^n$ for all $x\in(a-r,a+r)$.
There is some $r \gt 0$ such that $f(x) = \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty}\dfrac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}(x-a)^n$ for $x\in(a-r,a+r)$.
